Sample text:
---
When my mother sold the house, my brother wanted to take the pencil marks off the kitchen doorframe. He arrived with a pry bar wrapped in a beach towel.

“You can’t just remove part of the house,” I said.

“It’s trim, Annie. They sell it by the foot.”

What they did not sell by the foot was the afternoon I overtook him. I was eleven and he was fourteen. Our father measured us twice because Paul had begun to cry. On the wood beside my name, Dad had written, in his fussy all-capitals, VERIFIED.

The buyers were coming at noon for the keys. It was ten-thirty. Our mother sat at the kitchen table eating an orange over the sink, or as nearly over the sink as a person could manage without getting out of her chair.

“Ask them,” she said.

Paul considered this a failure of imagination. He had brought matching trim. He had brought white paint in a jam jar. He had even brought the tiny brush from his daughter’s watercolor set, its handle printed with yellow ducks.

“By the time they get here,” he said, “there won’t be anything to ask.”

He worked the flat end of the bar under the wood. The first nail came free with a squeak. Behind the strip was a narrow band of green wallpaper, a color so vigorous and unpleasant that all three of us said, “Oh,” and leaned closer.

“Your grandmother picked that,” Mom said.

“I thought Grandma had taste.”

“She did. She liked that.”

Paul eased out the second nail. Halfway up the frame, the wood split lengthwise. He stopped. A sliver stood out from the wall, bearing the top half of an E.

Mom put down her orange.

“I used to cheat,” she said.

Paul kept one hand on the bar. “At what?”

“When he measured you. I’d put my thumb under the book.”

“Which of us?”

“Whoever was having a bad year.”

Outside, the scrub jay that had spent the morning dismantling a patio cushion flew past the window with a long white thread in its beak.

“Eleven was a pretty bad year for me,” I said.

“It was,” she agreed.

“Fourteen was no picnic,” Paul said.

“You had the drums.”

“I was bad at the drums.”

“You didn’t know that then.”

He started laughing, which made the pry bar wobble, which made me grab the loose end of the trim. For a moment the two of us stood there holding it to the wall.

“I’ve got nowhere to put this,” he said.

Neither did I. My apartment doors were metal. Paul’s wife had spent two years renovating their house to look as little like the house we grew up in as money allowed.

Mom took the duck brush out of his pocket. “Put it back.”

We put it back. Paul tapped the nails in with the heel of his hand as far as they would go, then fetched his hammer. I fitted the splinter into place. Mom painted a thin white seam along the crack. She had a steadier hand than either of us, though lately she had asked me to write her checks.

At noon the buyers came: two women and a little boy in a red coat, too warm for the weather. While the adults dealt with keys and the garage code, he stood in the kitchen examining the pencil marks. Then he backed up to the frame, heels together, chin lifted. He did it so naturally I looked around for a pencil.

My mother already had one.

“May I?” she asked the women. They nodded. She found a paperback in her handbag and rested it on his head. He held himself very still.

“What’s your name, sweetheart?”

“Daniel.”

She drew the line and wrote DANIEL beside it, then handed his mothers the pencil. Paul carried her handbag to the car. I took the bag of oranges. We were halfway down the front walk when I thought to ask.

“Did you give him the thumb?”

Mom looked back. Through the kitchen window we could see Daniel jumping, trying to touch the top of the door.

“First day in a new house,” she said. “Absolutely.”
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet literary short story builds around a family’s attempt to preserve childhood height marks as they leave their old house.

## Grounded reading
The voice is restrained and observant, letting practical gestures carry the emotion: the pry bar, the duck-handled brush, the orange eaten over the sink. Its pathos comes from the family’s imperfect care for one another—especially the mother’s admission that she quietly adjusted the measurements when one child was having a bad year. The ending offers a gentle invitation to see inheritance not as a possession to take away, but as a small act of welcome that can be repeated for someone new.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds family memory, sibling rivalry, and the quiet accommodations parents make for children in pain. Objects hold that history: the marked doorframe, the concealed strip of wallpaper, the brush, and the mother’s pencil. The final gesture extends the family ritual to the next child, suggesting that what is passed on is less the house itself than the habit of making room for someone.

## Evidence line
> What they did not sell by the foot was the afternoon I overtook him.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story’s recurring objects, carefully restrained emotion, and resonant final gesture make its chosen literary sensibility distinct in this sample.
